resolution.method: EAS exact match on 222 02ND ST → parcel 3735063; sf-parcels has blklot 3735063 active, 222–222 02ND; the 2025 roll records it as commercial office, built 2016. resolution.note: Dated 1852, before the 1909 renumbering, and the record gives no cross street, block face or lot dimension to check the number against. EAS holds 222 SECOND today, but a pre-1909 number is not today's number until a cross-street check says so — see 'The renumbering traps' in research/RUNBOOK.md. Resolve it by hand if the source supplies the check material. The assessor dates the building on the parcel it would have resolved to (3735063) to 2016, 164 year(s) from the 1852 recorded here — far enough apart that the number probably points at a later building on the lot.

raw.text: The  site  is  on  Assessor's  Block  256,  Lot  16,  a  rectangular  corner  lot  containing  approximately  6,100  square  feet.  Currently,  the  site  is  vacant  although  it  is  paved  and  is  used  as  a  surface  parking  lot.

resolution.method: sf-eas-addresses has 897 CALIFORNIA ST but it does not join to one parcel. 897 CALIFORNIA ST's coordinates fall in 20 active parcels (0256102, 0256108, 0256106, 0256128…), which is what a condominium looks like in sf-parcels: one parcel per unit, none of them the building.

findings.address_as_written: the block bordered by Market, Mission, Beale, and Fremont ... the project site
findings.description: Before the 1850s the project block (Assessor's Block 3710, the site of the proposed 345 Market Street and 45 Fremont Street development) lay underwater in Yerba Buena Cove, where ships were scuttled and left to serve as warehouses and offices. A seawall was built along the present Embarcadero, the cove was filled in 1873, and the site was reclaimed by earthfilling between 1870 and 1875; buried ships reportedly remain, including the Byron, estimated to lie at the corner of Market and Beale Streets (citing the San Francisco News-Call Bulletin of July 16, 1964), and a Maritime Museum map also indicates a buried ship near Market and Beale. The South of Market area then became San Francisco's first industrial area.

citation.label: San Francisco Department of City Planning, *Draft Environmental Impact Report: Proposed High Rise Development at 345 Market Street and 45 Fremont Street*, 1975.
citation.locator: January 1975 draft (EE74.224; review period January 27-February 27, 1975); II. Environmental Setting, A. Earth and D. Cultural and Socioeconomic Factors, pp. 12-14; also III. Environmental Impact, H. Historical or Archeological Sites, p. 43

raw.text: Prior to the 1850's the general area of the project site was under water within San Francisco Bay. Between 1870 and 1875, a sea wall was constructed and the project site was reclaimed from the bay by earthfilling. ... a seawall was built along the present Embarcadero, Yerba Buena Cove was filled (1873) and the old ships were buried, including the Byron, which is estimated to be buried at the corner of Market and Beale Streets. ... A map at the Maritime Museum indicates that a buried ship lies in the vicinity of Market and Beale, but this has not been verified.

findings.description: Before the 1850s the project block (Assessor's Block 3710, the site of 345 Market Street and 45 Fremont Street) lay underwater in Yerba Buena Cove, where ships were scuttled and left to serve as warehouses and offices. A seawall was built along the present Embarcadero between 1870 and 1875, the cove was filled in 1873, and the site was reclaimed by earthfilling; buried ships reportedly remain, including the Byron, estimated to lie at the corner of Market and Beale Streets. The South of Market area then became San Francisco's first industrial area.

findings.description: The former Mobil Oil Bulk Terminal at 440 Jefferson Street, across Fish Alley south of Wharf J-10, operated petroleum storage tanks from sometime before 1935 through about 1946 and was succeeded by the still-active General Petroleum Marine Diesel Bulk Storage Facility; diesel pipelines from the site to the Hyde Street fuel docks traverse Wharf J-10. A 1990 release of several hundred gallons of petroleum occurred in the terminal's bermed tank yard, and Exxon/Mobil had monitored groundwater there since 1992 under a Regional Water Quality Control Board order.
